prompt: caio holds `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess`, which allows `s3:Get*` on every resource, and an inline policy denying `s3:*` on `shop-backups`. He asks for an object in `shop-backups`. What happens?
hint: Does specificity count?

choices.text: Allowed: `s3:Get*` names the action more precisely than `s3:*`
choices.why: Specificity decides nothing in IAM. An explicit `Deny` that matches ends the request.

choices.text: Refused: an explicit `Deny` that matches beats every `Allow`
choices.why: Right, and moto judged exactly this the way AWS does: `shop-assets` listed, `shop-backups` was refused.

choices.text: Allowed, because the managed policy was attached before the inline one
choices.why: Order of attachment, like order of statements, plays no part.

choices.text: It depends on which of the two policies AWS happens to read first
choices.why: AWS reads all of them together; the outcome is the same every time.

prompt: A brand-new IAM user with no policies runs `aws s3 ls` and is refused. What refused it?
hint: Nobody wrote anything about this user.

choices.text: A `Deny` that AWS attaches to every new user
choices.why: No policy is attached to a new user. The refusal needs none.

choices.text: Nothing allowed it
choices.why: Right: the implicit deny. It is where every request starts, and only an `Allow` moves it.

choices.text: S3 refuses every user who has no MFA device
choices.why: MFA matters only where a policy's condition asks for it.

choices.text: moto's count of free requests had run out
choices.why: Running out of the count is what makes moto judge; the judgement itself is the missing `Allow`.

prompt: An SCP on `shop-prod` allows `s3:*`. A role in that account has no identity policies, and the bucket it reads has no bucket policy. Can the role read the bucket?
hint: Which kind of layer is an SCP?

choices.text: Yes: the SCP allows it, and nothing denies it
choices.why: An SCP only limits. Its `Allow` says how far the account's policies may go, and here none goes anywhere.

choices.text: Yes, for buckets that belong to the same organisation
choices.why: Belonging to an organisation grants nothing either; a granting layer has to allow the action.

choices.text: No: nothing in a granting layer allows it
choices.why: Right. Passing every limit is half of the rule; the other half is an `Allow` in an identity or resource policy.

choices.text: No, because an SCP that allows something denies everything else to root
choices.why: The SCP caps every principal, root included, but it was not what refused this request: the missing grant was.

prompt: A role in `shop-prod` writes to `shop-logs`, a bucket in `log-archive`. The bucket policy allows the role; the role's own policies say nothing about S3. Is the write allowed?
hint: How many accounts are involved?

choices.text: Yes: a bucket policy that allows a principal is enough
choices.why: Within one account, it would be. Across accounts the caller's side has to allow it as well.

choices.text: No: the role's own side grants nothing
choices.why: Right. The role needs `s3:PutObject` on the bucket in its own policy too. That rule was not run here, since moto judges no bucket policy.

choices.text: Yes, since both accounts are in the shop's organisation
choices.why: Sharing an organisation grants nothing; each account's policies still decide.

choices.text: No: AWS forbids writing to another account's bucket
choices.why: It is allowed and common, as long as both sides grant it; central logging works exactly like this.

prompt: Put the steps of AWS's evaluation, as the lesson's figure draws them, in order.
hint: The step that can end everything at once comes first.
items: look for an explicit `Deny` in any policy
check that the organisation's SCPs and RCPs allow it
find an `Allow` in an identity or resource policy
check the permission boundary, if one is set
check the session policy, if one was passed
trap: Putting the `Allow` first is the usual slip. An `Allow` found early decides nothing, because a `Deny` or a limit later still refuses.

prompt: Match each layer to who writes it.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: an administrator, on a user or role

right_distractors: AWS, the same for every account

prompt: A user has no policies of his own and a permission boundary of `s3:*`. In AWS, can he list the buckets?
hint: Intersection or sum?

choices.text: Yes: the boundary allows every S3 action
choices.why: A boundary grants nothing. Its `Allow` is a ceiling, and with no identity policy there is nothing under it.

choices.text: No: the intersection of nothing and S3 is nothing
choices.why: Right. The boundary only removes; an identity policy still has to allow the listing.

choices.text: Yes, but only for buckets he created himself
choices.why: Creating a bucket grants its creator nothing in IAM, and he could not have created one anyway.

choices.text: Only after the boundary propagates, a few minutes later
choices.why: Timing is not the issue; no amount of waiting turns a ceiling into a grant.

prompt: `app-admin` holds `AdministratorAccess` and an S3-only boundary. A session of it calls `iam:ListUsers`. What would AWS answer, and what did moto answer?
hint: moto stores boundaries.

choices.text: Both list the users: `AdministratorAccess` is above any boundary
choices.why: No policy is above a boundary; that is what a boundary is for. Only moto listed them.

choices.text: Both refuse, because moto applies the boundary as AWS does
choices.why: moto stores the boundary and never applies it: the session listed `admin`, `caio` and `dani`.

choices.text: AWS refuses; moto listed every user
choices.why: Right. `iam:ListUsers` is outside the intersection, so AWS refuses it. The refusal was not run here.

choices.text: AWS lists them; moto refused, because the boundary names S3
choices.why: It is the other way round: AWS applies boundaries and moto does not.

prompt: Which of these did moto ignore in this lesson, though AWS would apply them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them it judged exactly as AWS does.

choices.text: A permission boundary on a role
choices.why: Right. Stored, and never applied.

choices.text: An explicit `Deny` in an inline user policy
choices.why: That one moto applied: `shop-backups` was refused to caio.

choices.text: A session policy passed to `assume-role`
choices.why: Right. Even a `Deny` on every IAM action changed nothing.

choices.text: A bucket policy denying the bucket's deletion
choices.why: Right. The bucket was deleted.

choices.text: The implicit deny for a user with no policy
choices.why: moto refused caio everything before any policy was attached, as AWS would.

choices.text: A condition demanding MFA
choices.why: Right. dani listed the buckets with a plain key.

prompt: Why is it dangerous to let a developer create roles and attach any policy to them, with no boundary in the way?
hint: What could the developer make, and then become?

choices.text: Every role costs money for as long as it exists
choices.why: Roles are free. The cost is in what one can be made to do.

choices.text: A role they make would turn them into administrators
choices.why: Right: create it, trust yourself, assume it. The boundary is what caps every role such a developer makes.

choices.text: Two developers might create roles with the same name
choices.why: IAM refuses a duplicate name; that is a nuisance, not an escalation.

choices.text: A role skips the MFA its creator was required to use
choices.why: Whether MFA is demanded depends on conditions, not on the role existing.

prompt: In the delegation policy, why does the second statement deny `iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary` and `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` on the boundary?
hint: What could a developer do just after creating a role correctly?

choices.text: To keep the boundary under the limit of five versions
choices.why: The limit of five is enforced anyway. The deny is about who may change the boundary at all.

choices.text: Because every `Allow` in a policy needs a matching `Deny`
choices.why: No such rule exists; most policies have no `Deny` at all.

choices.text: So the cap cannot be removed or rewritten afterwards
choices.why: Right. The first statement makes the boundary the price of a role; the second stops the price being taken back.

choices.text: To stop developers deleting the roles they created
choices.why: `DeleteRole` is not in the list; deleting a role of one's own is harmless here.

prompt: The condition key a delegation policy uses to demand a ceiling on every new role is `iam:___`.
hint: It names the managed policy given in the request.

prompt: A role's identity policies allow `s3:*` and `iam:*`. Its boundary allows `s3:*` and `logs:*`. Of the three services S3, IAM and CloudWatch Logs, how many can its sessions use in AWS?
hint: The overlap of the two lists.

prompt: `shop-assets` has a bucket policy denying `s3:DeleteBucket` to `"*"`. In AWS, `admin`, holding `AdministratorAccess` in the same account, empties the bucket and deletes it. What happens?
hint: Where does an explicit `Deny` count?

choices.text: Deleted: an administrator is above a bucket policy
choices.why: Nothing is above an explicit `Deny`, `AdministratorAccess` included.

choices.text: Deleted: a bucket policy applies only to other accounts
choices.why: It applies to whoever it names, and `"*"` names everybody, the owner's principals included.

choices.text: Refused: the explicit `Deny` ends the request wherever it is written
choices.why: Right. moto deleted it, since it never reads bucket policies; AWS's refusal was not run here.

choices.text: Refused, until admin first deletes the bucket policy, which he cannot
choices.why: He can delete the policy, since nothing denies that, and then the bucket. The `Deny` guards against accidents, not against a determined administrator.

prompt: A policy denies everything when `{"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "false"}}`. In AWS, a script signs a request with a long-term access key and no MFA. Is the request denied by that statement?
hint: Is the key `false`, or absent?

choices.text: No: for a long-term key the MFA key is absent
choices.why: Right. That is why the documented form is `BoolIfExists`, which also matches a missing key.

choices.text: Yes: with no MFA, the key's value is `false`
choices.why: For a long-term key the key is not present at all, which is the trap.

choices.text: Yes, and moto would deny it the same way
choices.why: moto treats every condition as met, so it would deny; AWS would not. They differ here.

choices.text: The policy is refused as malformed, since `Bool` takes no strings
choices.why: `"false"` is how a boolean value is written in a condition; the document is valid.

prompt: A bucket allows reads only with `IpAddress` on `aws:SourceIp` `203.0.113.0/24`, the office. An application on an EC2 machine reaches S3 through a VPC endpoint and is refused. Why?
hint: What does the request through the endpoint carry?

choices.text: The machine's public address is outside the office range
choices.why: Through an endpoint there is no public address in the request at all.

choices.text: VPC endpoints do not support S3
choices.why: S3 is one of the commonest endpoints; lesson 19 builds one.

choices.text: Conditions are not evaluated for requests from EC2
choices.why: They are evaluated for every request. This one simply lacks the key.

choices.text: The request carries no public address to compare
choices.why: Right. The endpoint has keys of its own, and a policy meant for both paths names both.

prompt: Match each condition key to what it holds.
hint: The table of four keys.

pairs.right: the public address the request came from
whether the credentials were obtained with MFA
a tag on the calling user or role
the region the request is for

right_distractors: the region the caller is in

prompt: Which tool says, for a principal and a list of actions, whether each would be allowed and which statement decided, without making the requests?
hint: One tool simulates; the others validate or survey.

choices.text: `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy`
choices.why: It checks one document's grammar and practice, not what a principal may do.

choices.text: `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`
choices.why: Right. It reads the principal's real policies and answers per action; moto answers it with HTTP 500, so it runs against AWS.

choices.text: An Access Analyzer for external access
choices.why: It lists resources shared outside the account or organisation, not decisions for one principal.

choices.text: `aws iam get-account-summary`
choices.why: It counts users, policies and quotas; it judges nothing.

prompt: In moto, a `Deny` limited to regions other than `sa-east-1` refused caio a request in `sa-east-1`. Why?
hint: What does moto do with a condition?

choices.text: `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` was set to another region
choices.why: The transcript printed `sa-east-1` just before the request.

choices.text: moto treats every condition as met, so the `Deny` applied
choices.why: Right. AWS would have compared the region and let the request through.

choices.text: Listing buckets is a global call, so its region is `us-east-1`
choices.why: A plausible worry, but moto never compared any region: removing the policy let the same call through.

choices.text: caio had no `Allow` for listing buckets
choices.why: He had `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess`; once the `Deny` was removed, the listing worked.

prompt: The shop wants a guarantee that nobody in `shop-prod`, its root user included, can stop CloudTrail. Which layer can give it?
hint: Which layer reaches the root user of a member account?

choices.text: A `Deny` in an identity policy on every user and role
choices.why: Root takes no identity policy, and every new identity would need the policy too.

choices.text: A permission boundary on every role in the account
choices.why: A boundary is set per identity, root cannot have one, and a role made tomorrow would start without it.

choices.text: A service control policy with a `Deny`, set by the organisation
choices.why: Right. An SCP caps every principal of the account, root and identities not yet created included; lesson 4 builds one.

choices.text: A session policy passed whenever somebody assumes a role
choices.why: A session policy is chosen by the caller, so it guarantees nothing about callers who leave it out.

prompt: A developer tests a new policy in the lab with moto's checking on, sees the call allowed, and concludes AWS will allow it too. What is the strongest reason that does not follow?
hint: What did moto skip in this lesson that could have refused the call?

choices.text: moto's keys are not real, so nothing it allows counts
choices.why: The keys are moto's, but the identity policies were judged as AWS judges them. The gap is elsewhere.

choices.text: moto applies no boundary, SCP or resource policy and treats every condition as met
choices.why: Right. Any of those could refuse in AWS what moto allowed; the simulator and Access Analyzer are where to find out.

choices.text: moto evaluates statements in order, and AWS does not
choices.why: Neither has an order; moto's explicit deny beat an allow exactly as AWS's does.

choices.text: A moto restart would have changed the answer
choices.why: A restart empties moto; it does not change how it judges a policy.

prompt: Every request to AWS starts as an implicit ___.
hint: The answer before any policy is read.
